How does a sampler make sound?

A guide for musicians taking their first look inside a sampler. It explains the sound engineering we learned while building the free plugin flipper, at a musician's level. It talks less about which button to press and more about why a sampler behaves the way it does. You don't need any maths or coding to read it.

About this guide

Who is it for? Anyone who wants to make beats but doesn't yet know what happens inside a sampler.

What will you get out of it? You'll be able to explain for yourself how sound gets cut, how pitch and speed change, and why old samplers sound the way they do. Words from gear manuals like , , and mid/side won't feel strange any more.

How should you read it? Each chapter takes one question and works through it, and ends with ways to hear it for yourself in flipper. Read from the start or jump to the chapter you're curious about. You can skip the "Go deeper" parts.

The big picture Sound comes in from a microphone or a record, goes through the sampler inside the computer, and out of a speaker. This guide follows that path in order.

1

From sound to electricity

Key questionHow does a microphone turn sound into electricity?

Sound is a vibration of the air. The air pressure goes up and down very quickly. A microphone catches this vibration and turns it into electricity, and a speaker takes that electricity and turns it back into vibration. Let's open both up first.

A microphone and a speaker work the same way. Inside the round grille of a dynamic microphone there's a thin plate (the diaphragm), a coil (wire wound round and round) stuck to the back of the plate, and a magnet. When the air pushes the diaphragm, the coil moves back and forth next to the magnet, and that makes electricity in the coil. This electricity travels out down the cable.

A speaker is almost the same inside. It has a magnet, a coil and a diaphragm, and only works in the other direction. Take the grille off the front of a speaker and the round plate you see in the middle is the diaphragm. When electricity flows into the coil, the magnet pushes and pulls it, and the diaphragm attached to it moves back and forth and pushes the air. A microphone makes electricity from air, and a speaker moves air with electricity. That's why a speaker wired the other way round can pick up sound like a microphone. Studios sometimes stand a big speaker in front of a kick drum instead of a mic for exactly this reason.

Now let's see how a speaker's diaphragm moves the air. When the diaphragm comes forward, it pushes the air right in front of it and squeezes it tight. When it goes back, the air loosens and spreads out.

This squeeze and loosen is passed to the next bit of air, then the next, all the way to your ear. Watch the orange grains in the animation below. Each grain of air only rocks a little back and forth in place along the direction the sound travels, and doesn't go anywhere (in real life it moves much less than the width of a hair). In fact, air grains are never still, even when there's no sound. They fly around very fast in every direction and bump into each other. Sound is a small back-and-forth push and pull added on top of that messy motion. What travels forward is the pattern of squeezed and loose places. When this pattern reaches your ear, a thin skin inside it (the eardrum) vibrates the same way, and we hear that vibration as sound.

A vibration can change in two ways.

  • How fast it vibrates: the number of vibrations per second is called the , written in Hz (hertz). The faster it vibrates, the higher the note sounds. The A in the middle of a piano (A4) vibrates 440 times a second. The A one up is exactly twice that, 880 Hz.
  • How strongly it vibrates: how hard the air is pushed and pulled. The stronger the vibration, the louder the sound.

Try it below. This is the simplest vibration there is, a sine wave. It starts quiet, but if you're wearing headphones, turn your volume down first.

The electricity inside a microphone vibrates in the same shape as the air. Like the eardrum, the microphone's diaphragm follows the air's vibration exactly. The further the diaphragm is pushed, the stronger the electricity, and the less it's pushed, the weaker, so the electricity in the wire rises and falls in the same shape as the air. When recording gear talks about a "signal", this electrical vibration is what it means.

Before computers, this shape was carved in as it was. On tape it's stored as the strength of magnetism, and on a record as a wiggly groove. To listen, the carved shape is turned back into electricity and sent to a speaker. Because it copies the shape of the vibration without any breaks, it's called analog recording.

But a computer can't hold a shape that flows on without breaks. All a computer can hold is numbers. So the vibration is turned into numbers, in the way we'll see in the next chapter.

flipper: try it

  • Load a sample and zoom far into the . The line going up and down is the shape the microphone's diaphragm vibrated in.
  • In mode, raise the pitch to +12. The same sound plays twice as fast, so the vibration is twice as fast too and you hear it one octave higher.
Go deeperWhat does an audio interface do?

The electrical signal from a microphone is very weak, so first a turns it up. Then an (analog-to-digital converter) turns the electrical vibration into numbers and sends them to the computer. When you listen, it goes the other way: a (digital-to-analog converter) turns the numbers back into an electrical vibration and sends it to your headphones or speakers. An audio interface is these three in one box.

Microphones come in two kinds too. A dynamic microphone makes its own electricity, like in the picture above, with a coil on the diaphragm moving next to a magnet. It's tough and handles loud sounds well, so it's used a lot on stage and on drums. A condenser microphone has no coil or magnet. Instead it reads the electrical change between a very thin diaphragm and a metal plate right behind it. It picks up quiet sounds and high notes in fine detail, but needs its own power, so you have to switch on the interface's (48 V).

In three lines
  • Sound is a vibration of the air.
  • Vibrations per second is the frequency. Double it and you go up an octave.
  • A microphone and a speaker are the same parts working in opposite directions.
2

Sound is numbers

Key questionHow does a computer hold sound?

As we saw in the last chapter, sound that has passed through a microphone is an electrical vibration. A computer measures how big this vibration is at very short, steady gaps and writes each measurement down as a number. Each of these numbers is a sample, and joining them up gives the you see on screen.

There are two things to decide here.

  • : how many times to measure each second. A CD measures 44,100 times a second (44.1 ). The more often you measure, the higher the sounds you can hold, because high sounds vibrate fast. There's one rule: the highest sound you can hold is half the sample rate. At 44.1 kHz that's about 22 kHz, which covers everything people can hear (about 20 kHz).
  • : how fine the ruler is for each measurement. 16 bits splits the level into 65,536 steps, and 12 bits into 4,096 steps. The coarser the steps, the more quiet sounds get smeared and noise creeps in. Each extra bit lets you hold sounds about 6 quieter.

A rising sine wave. Measured at 8 kHz, the highest sound it can hold (the Nyquist frequency) is 4 kHz. Without a filter, the moment it passes 4 kHz the sound turns round and goes down (aliasing). With the filter, everything above 4 kHz simply disappears.

One thick synth note with fewer and fewer steps on the ruler. You hear the biggest difference at the end, where the sound gets quiet.

Old samplers were made when memory was expensive, so they saved on both. The SP-1200, released in 1987, measured about 26,000 times a second at 12 bits and only held sound up to about 13 kHz. What was missing ended up becoming that machine's own sound. We come back to this in chapter 7.

flipper: try it

  • When you load a sample, its length and sample rate (for example 44.1 kHz) show under the file name.
  • Switch the engine from clean to black. black is modelled on a 26 kHz, 12-bit machine, so the highs drop and the sound gets rougher.
Go deeperWhat is the Nyquist frequency?

The Nyquist frequency is the highest sound a sample rate can hold. It's exactly half the sample rate. At 44.1 kHz it's 22.05 kHz, and measuring at about 26 kHz like the SP-1200 it's about 13 kHz.

Why half? One vibration goes up once and comes down once. To spot that vibration from numbers alone, you need to measure at least twice: once near the top and once near the bottom. So measuring 44,100 times a second, you can only recognise sounds that vibrate up to 22,050 times a second.

If you measure a sound that vibrates faster than that, the dots land too far apart, and joining them draws a wrong, slower vibration. It's the same thing that makes a car's wheels in a video seem to turn slowly backwards when they spin fast. This is the we'll see in chapter 7. That's why recording gear has a filter that shaves off sounds above the Nyquist frequency before measuring (an anti-aliasing filter). Old samplers had a weak filter or none at all, so the wrong sounds were recorded in, and that became the flavour of those machines.

Go deeperWhy 6 dB per bit?

One more bit makes the steps on the ruler twice as fine. That means a sound half as big as before can now be held without getting lost in the steps. And sound level has a rule: "half the size is 6 dB quieter" (chapter 11 shows why it's 6). So each bit adds 6 dB: 16 bits holds 6 × 16 = about 96 dB, and 24 bits about 144 dB. That's the distance from the loudest sound down to the quietest sound that doesn't get lost in the steps.

Recording at 24 bits gives you room to spare. Even if you record quietly because you're afraid of , there are plenty of steps at the bottom, so quiet sounds don't get smeared. A finished song is fine at 16 bits. When you bring it down to 16 bits, though, you mix in a tiny bit of noise (dither). That gets rid of the harsh stepped sound and leaves only a very quiet, even hiss like tape hiss.

In three lines
  • A computer measures the electrical vibration very often and writes it down as numbers.
  • Measurements per second is the sample rate; how fine the ruler is, is the bit depth.
  • The highest sound it can hold is half the sample rate.
3

Samples and samplers

Key questionHow is a sampler different from a synthesizer?

A builds sound from scratch. It shapes simple waveforms with filters and envelopes into sounds that never existed. A sampler records sounds that already exist and plays them like an instrument. When you press a key or pad, it reads the recorded numbers again and sends them out as sound. So what a sampler can do comes down to how freely it can read a recording again: where to start reading, how fast to read, whether to read it backwards, and so on.

A short history

Hip-hop producers used these machines to record drum breaks and phrases from records, cut them up and rearrange them. Memory only lasted a few seconds, and the tricks they came up with (like recording a record at a faster speed) set into the sound of the genre. The most-used originals are collected under "Famous samples to listen to" in the appendix.

Chop and flip Chopping is cutting a sample into pieces, and flipping is rearranging those pieces in a new order and rhythm until it's a completely different song from the original. That's where the name flipper comes from.

flipper: try it

  • Drag in one sample, play the pads in order, then play them in a different order. That's your first flip.
Go deeperHow does a sampler read a recording again?

A sampler reads the recorded numbers one after another. Which number it's reading right now is called the playhead. At the original speed the playhead moves forward one step at a time. One up, it moves two steps at a time, and one up, about 1.059 steps.

When the playhead lands between two steps, like at 1.059, there's no number written there. So it looks at the numbers before and after and guesses the value in between. This is called . The simplest way is to just use the nearest number, and a better way is to smoothly connect several numbers on either side.

Interpolation and are different things, but they're linked. Interpolation is the calculation that fills in the values between, and aliasing is the result when rough sounds that were never there appear. Sloppy interpolation (skipping or repeating numbers) makes more aliasing. It's one of the places where old machines and modern samplers sound different (chapter 7).

A loop is the playhead going back to the start point when it reaches the end point, and reverse is the playhead moving backwards. Almost every sampler feature can be explained by where the playhead moves, how fast, and in which direction.

In three lines
  • A sampler reads a recording again and plays it like an instrument.
  • Chopping is cutting; flipping is rearranging the pieces in a new order.
  • Values between two steps are filled in from the numbers on either side (interpolation).
4

Cutting

Key questionWhere should you cut a sound so it sounds natural?

Most sounds start with a sharp hit and slowly away. Kicks, snares and pianos all do. This starting moment is called the . Cut right before the transient and the sound comes out clean when you hit the pad. Cut a little late and the head of the sound is lost, so it loses its punch. Cut too early and the tail of the sound before it comes along too.

How does a machine find transients? It cuts the sound into very short pieces, measures how strong each piece is, and looks for places that suddenly get louder than the piece just before. It doesn't only look at loudness; it also looks for places where a new tone colour jumps out. How clear a jump has to be before it counts as a transient is set by the . Turn it up and even quiet hi-hats are caught; turn it down and only the big kicks and snares are left.

Three ways to cut

  • By transient: the method described above. It suits drum loops and clear playing.
  • By beat (grid): if you know the tempo, you know how long one beat is. At 90 one beat is 60 ÷ 90 ≈ 0.67 seconds. Cutting at exactly these gaps splits even pads and strings with soft transients neatly on the beat.
  • By hand (): you listen to the sound and tap a key at the moment you want to cut. Human hands are always a little early or late, so a good lazy chop finds the most likely transient near the moment you tapped and snaps to it.

Why do you hear a "tick"? A is a line that goes up and down. If you cut it suddenly where the line is far from the middle, the speaker jumps in an instant and you hear a "tick" click. There are two ways to stop it.

  • Fade: turn the sound down over a very short time at the cut, so the end comes down to 0.
  • : a spot where the waveform passes through the middle line (0). Nudge the cut to the nearest zero crossing and the end is at 0, so it doesn't jump.

flipper: try it

  • When you open a sample, flipper finds the transients ahead of time. Turn the sensitivity knob and watch how the markers change.
  • Switch to grid and cut at 1/8 and 1/4, and listen to how the two methods differ.
  • Turn on lazy chop and hit any pad while you listen. It cuts at the transient nearest the moment you hit.
  • When you move the end of a slice, turn on the magnet and it snaps to a zero crossing.
Go deeperHow is transient finding actually calculated?

The sound is cut into pieces tens of milliseconds long (frames), and each 's frequencies are worked out with a fast Fourier transform (FFT, see the next fold-out). Then for each band it measures how much louder it got than in the frame just before, and adds up only the increases. Anything that got quieter is thrown away. This value is called spectral flux, and it shoots up the moment a new sound comes in.

If you only look at the overall level, it's easy to miss a hi-hat that comes in while a bass is ringing long. Looking band by band, you can catch a new sound appearing up in the highs on its own, so it's more accurate.

Last, it chooses which of the jumps count as transients. A single fixed line would miss transients in quiet parts, so it usually looks at how much higher each jump is than the average around it. Sensitivity is the handle that sets this "how much".

Go deeperWhat is a fast Fourier transform (FFT)?

Any sound is many simple vibrations stacked together. This idea comes from the French mathematician Fourier in the early 1800s. When you play a single A on a piano, it isn't just one 440 Hz vibration. Vibrations at 440, 880, 1320 Hz … are stacked, each at a different level. The mix of these levels is the tone colour. It's why the same A sounds different on a piano and a guitar.

A Fourier transform untangles the stack. Put in a waveform (a line that rises and falls over time) and it tells you which frequencies are inside and how strong each one is (the ). It moves a signal from a time axis to a frequency axis. The dancing bar chart on an EQ screen (a spectrum analyser) is the result of this calculation.

How does it find them? The idea is "hold it up and compare". Make a sine wave at the frequency you want to check, line it up with the sound, multiply them point by point and add it all up. If that frequency is in the sound, the two rise and fall together and the total comes out large. If it isn't, they agree half the time and disagree half the time, cancel each other out, and the total comes out close to 0. Repeat this for every frequency and the list is complete.

So what's "fast" about it? Done directly, it's far too much work. Comparing 1,024 samples with 1,024 frequencies one by one takes over a million multiplications. The fast Fourier transform is a trick that gets the same answer with much less work. It splits the samples into even and odd halves, solves each half separately, then splits those halves again, and so on. That way shared work only has to be done once, which brings it down to about 10,000 multiplications, around 100 times faster. Cooley and Tukey made the method widely known in 1965, and it's what lets computers analyse sound in real time.

It has limits too. Feed it short pieces and it knows exactly "when" a sound happened but only roughly which frequency. Feed it long pieces and it tells frequencies apart finely but "when" gets blurry. You can't have top and top at once. That's why transient finding uses short pieces and key finding uses long ones. It's also why the in chapter 5 looks at high sounds in short pieces and low sounds in long ones.

Go deeperHow are a fade and a zero crossing different?

Both aim for the same thing: making the waveform touch the middle line (0) at the cut, so the speaker doesn't jump. Only the method is different.

A fade changes the sound. It turns the sound down over the last few milliseconds before the cut, pulling the end down to 0. You can cut anywhere, but if the fade is too long the end of the sound gets blurry.

A zero crossing moves the cut. A waveform keeps passing through the middle line as it goes up and down, and at that instant its level is 0. You nudge the cut a little earlier or later to that instant. The sound stays as it was, but the cut moves slightly away from where you first wanted it.

That's why the two are often used together. First snap to a zero crossing, then wipe out any small jump that's left with a very short fade.

Go deeperHow short should a fade be?

A click is a short sound made when the waveform breaks off in an instant, so it has everything from lows to highs mixed in. A short fade of about 1–5 milliseconds gets rid of almost all of it, and that's not long enough to soften the attack. If the fade is too long, the "thump" at the head of a kick gets blurry, so keep fades short on drums and a little longer on pads and vocals.

In three lines
  • Cut right before the transient and it comes out clean.
  • Cut just anywhere and you hear a "tick".
  • A fade or a zero crossing brings the cut end to 0.
5

Pitch and speed

Key questionWhy does raising the pitch make it faster?

Spin a record faster by hand and the gets higher and faster. Pitch is set by , that is, how many times per second something vibrates. Play a recording faster and the same vibrations happen in less time, so pitch and speed change together. A sampler works the same way. Read the stored numbers faster and it gets higher and faster; read them slower and it gets lower and slower. This is called .

In numbers, to go up one you read about 1.059 times faster (¹²√2). Multiply that twelve times and you get exactly 2, which is one . So going up an octave halves the length, and a 90 loop becomes 180 BPM. Going down an octave does the opposite: the length doubles and the loop becomes 45 BPM. Going down just 2 semitones gives about 80 BPM.

33 and 45 A record turns 33⅓ or 45 times a minute. Playing a 33⅓ record at 45 makes it about 1.35 times faster, roughly 5 semitones higher. Back when sampler memory was only a few seconds, producers played records at 45 to fit more in, then played them back lower in the sampler. It saved memory, but the highs got rougher, and that rough flavour became a colour of its own.

Can you change only the pitch and keep the speed? Yes. It's called . The sound is split into small pieces tens of milliseconds long. To slow it down, the pieces are spread a little further apart and overlapped; to speed it up, they're overlapped more tightly. Each piece plays at the original speed, so the pitch stays the same. To change only the pitch, you repitch (changing pitch and speed together), then stretch the speed back to where it was.

Repitch changes pitch and speed together. Stretch changes only one of them. The stretch was rendered ahead of time with Rubber Band R3, the same one flipper uses.

🎧 Listenpress again to stop

melody notes (higher = higher pitch) where they were beats

So why does the sound get smeared? If the doesn't line up where the pieces overlap, the sound wobbles or gets metallic. Drums get especially mushy when a is spread across several pieces. A good stretch algorithm lines up each piece's (where the waveform is in its cycle) when joining, and leaves transients as they are instead of stretching them.

flipper: try it

  • In repitch, lower the key to −2 and watch what happens to the BPM. Key and speed move together.
  • Switch to keep tempo and the tempo stays while only the key changes.
  • On a drum loop, turn 'crisp' on and off. When it's on, the start of each transient is kept exactly as the original.
  • In grey, black and purple you can set the record speed to 45 or 78. Key and tempo stay the same; only the highs get rougher.
Go deeperWhere does ¹²√2 come from?

Today's instruments split an octave into twelve semitones with equal spacing (). Going up an octave doubles the frequency, so one semitone has to go up by "the number that makes 2 when you multiply it twelve times". That number is ¹²√2, about 1.059. So each semitone up means reading 1.059 times faster. 7 semitones up is about 1.5 times, and one octave down is 0.5 times.

The other way round, if you know how many times faster something is, you can work out how many semitones it is. Playing a 33⅓ record at 45 makes it 1.35 times faster. Count how many times you need to multiply 1.059 to reach 1.35 and it's a little over five. That's why we said "roughly 5 semitones". (As a formula: semitones = 12 × log2(ratio).)

Go deeperWhat kinds of time stretch are there?

There are two main families. One overlaps and joins pieces of the waveform as they are (the time domain). When overlapping, it searches a little for a spot where the waveforms line up well. It holds up well on clear sounds like drums and voices, but wobbles easily on complex chords.

The other stretches in the frequency domain (a ). It untangles the sound into frequencies with the fast Fourier transform from chapter 4, stretches each one with its phase lined up, and puts them back together. It holds up well on chords and pads, but transients get spread out, drums go mushy, and you easily get a typical muffled ringing.

A good stretch algorithm uses each method to cover the other's weak spots. It leaves transients unstretched, and looks at high sounds in short pieces and low sounds in long ones separately. Rubber Band R3, which flipper uses, works with several windows of different lengths like this.

In three lines
  • Repitch changes pitch and speed together.
  • Time stretch changes only one of them.
  • One semitone is about 1.059×; twelve of them make exactly 2×.
6

Finding the key and tempo

Key questionHow do you work out a sample's key and BPM?

The key is found in three steps.

  1. Collect the notes. Going through the sample in short pieces, it collects how strongly each of the twelve notes rings: C, C#, D … B. Octaves don't matter, so a low C and a high C both count as "C". This twelve-bar chart is called the .
  2. Compare with the tables. Every key has notes it uses a lot. A song in C major uses C, E and G a lot and hardly ever uses C#. Music researchers counted a huge number of real songs and made tables of how often each of the 24 keys (12 major and 12 minor) uses each note. These tables are called key profiles.
  3. Pick the closest key. It holds the sample's chroma up against each of the 24 tables, and picks the key whose shape matches best.

A closer look at the chroma. A piano has 88 keys, but only twelve names repeat: C, C#, D … B. A low C and a high C are exactly double in (one ), so to the ear they're the same note. The chroma uses this: it ignores how high a note is and only collects how much each of the twelve names rang.

For example, if the bass plays a low C and the piano plays a C, E, G chord, the low C and the middle C both pile up in the "C" bar. So the C bar is tallest, E and G come next, and the other nine bars stay empty.

Collect this over a whole song and you can see at a glance which notes it's made of. Key finding looks at this shape and decides "lots of C, E and G, almost no C#, so probably C major". The chroma keeps no order or rhythm of the notes. So songs made of the same notes have similar chromas even with different melodies, which makes it a good fit for looking at a song's note material as a whole.

Why does it get it wrong? C major and A minor use exactly the same notes, so they're easy to mix up. A short loop has few notes, so there isn't enough to judge from, and sounds without a clear pitch, like drums, don't fit any table well. That's why good key-finding programs show several candidates, and leave the key blank when they aren't sure.

Records that are out of tune Standard tuning puts A at 440 Hz. But old records are sometimes a little off because of tape speed or how the instruments were tuned. A split into 100 steps is called a , and if you measure how many cents all twelve notes are pushed the same way, you know how far off the record is. When you add another instrument, tune it by that much.

Finding the It looks for the gap at which transients repeat. It slides the graph along bit by bit, lays it over the original, and takes the gap where they overlap best as one beat. But machines often mix up half and double, like 90 and 180 or 120 and 60, because both fit the beat. If the file name says "90 bpm" or the loop is exactly two bars long, trust that instead.

flipper: try it

  • When you open a sample, the key chip shows the original key and the key you're hearing now, like 'Am → Gm'. Turning the key knob changes the second one.
  • Press the key chip to see other candidates. Switch straight between the easily confused major and minor and listen.
  • Press the BPM to see candidates guessed from the file name and length.
Go deeperHow is the chroma made?

First the is worked out with the fast Fourier transform (FFT) from chapter 4. Then for each frequency it finds which note that is. 440 Hz is A, and each semitone up multiplies the frequency by 1.059, so if you know the frequency you can count back to the note. Octaves are thrown away here, leaving only names like C, C#, D ….

Add up the strength of everything with the same note name and the twelve bars fill up. Do this for each short piece and add them up from the start of the sample to the end, and the bar chart shows which notes the sample is made of.

Go deeperHow is the closest key chosen?

It measures how alike the chroma (12 bars) and a (12 bars) are in shape using a . Where one is high and the other is high too, it gets close to 1; where they disagree it goes to 0 or below. Rotating the C major profile one step gives C# major, D major and so on, so one major profile and one minor profile are each rotated twelve times to give 24 scores, and the highest key wins.

Key profiles started with an experiment by Krumhansl and Kessler in 1982. They played people chords in a key, then a single note, and asked them to score how well the note fit. Those scores became the first key profiles. Later, Albrecht and Shanahan built profiles by counting notes directly in the scores of many pieces instead of using people's ratings, and these get minor keys right more often.

Go deeperHow is BPM measured?

The transient graph from chapter 4 is slid sideways bit by bit and laid over the original, and each position gets a score for how well they overlap (). In a song with a transient on every beat, the score shoots up when it's slid by exactly one beat. That amount of time is one beat, and BPM = 60 ÷ one beat (in seconds).

But sliding by two beats, or by half a beat, also overlaps quite well. That's how 90 and 180, or 120 and 60, get mixed up. Usually common tempos (say 70–160) get a little bonus, and it also checks whether the loop length divides neatly into bars.

In three lines
  • The key is found from how much each of the twelve notes rings.
  • The tempo is found from the gap at which transients repeat.
  • Major vs minor, and half vs double tempo, often fool machines.
7

The sound of old samplers

Key questionWhy do old machines sound good?

Old samplers weren't made rough on purpose. Memory and parts were expensive, so they saved everywhere they could, and the traces of that stayed in the sound. As classic albums made on those machines piled up, those traces became the sound of the genre. There are four main ones.

  • : in chapter 2 we said a sound above half the can't be held. If such a sound isn't filtered out first, it folds back down to a lower place, like a reflection in a mirror. Notes that were never there appear and the sound gets rough and metallic.
  • Coarse steps: with few bits, quiet sounds get smeared into steps, and the tail of the sound turns gritty.
  • How the speed is changed: modern samplers read smoothly between samples. Some old machines skipped samples to go higher and read the same sample twice to go lower. That makes more aliasing.
  • Analog circuits: the filters and amps the sound goes through after the numbers are turned back into electricity differ from machine to machine, so the way the highs are cut and how warm it sounds differ too.

Listen on a bright piano loop: the more high sound there is, the easier the difference is to hear. The third one is the old trick of sampling the record sped up and playing it back lower on the sampler. The pitch is the same as the original, but even less high sound fits and there is more grit. This only imitates the sample rate and bits; flipper's black and grey engines add the filters and the character of the circuits too.

Three machines flipper is modelled on

EngineModelled onWhat makes the sound
black1987 E-mu SP-1200About 26 , 12 bits. It skips or repeats samples when the pitch changes. Outputs 1–2 have a moving filter (opens when hit, closes over about 0.1 seconds), and outputs 3–6 have fixed filters.
grey1988 Akai MPC6040 kHz, 12 bits. It stores sound on a , so quiet sounds get fine steps and loud sounds coarse ones. A filter cuts the highs around 18 kHz.
purple1990 Nintendo SNES (Super Famicom)About 32 kHz. It squeezes each group of 16 samples into 4 bits. On playback, smooths the sound into a soft blur, and the board's filter cuts once more.

The SP-1200's moving filter Every time you hit a pad, the filter opens wide and slowly closes. The head of the sound is bright and the tail darker, so it sounds like a real drum, and the noise in the tail gets buried too. flipper read the values from the circuit diagrams in the service manual and copied them over exactly.

Why the SNES sounds muffled The SNES only had 64 KB of memory for sound. So it packed each group of 16 samples into 4 bits each, and on playback it blended 4 samples to join them smoothly. That blending smears the highs, which gives it its soft, muffled sound.

So why does it sound good? There's no single answer, but here are a few reasons. With fewer highs, sound feels thicker and closer. Aliasing and noise add attack and a sticky feel to drums. And above all, the classic records we love were made with that sound, so our ears remember it as hip-hop.

flipper: try it

  • Play the same slice on clean, black, grey and purple in turn. The screen's skin changes to match each machine too.
  • On black, raise the key a lot. You hear the rough sound of samples being skipped. clean stays clean at the same key.
  • Change black's filter and compare the moving filter with a fixed one.
Go deeperWhere does the folded sound land?

In the chapter 2 animation, measuring a vibration that's too fast made a wrong orange vibration. You can easily work out how many kHz that wrong sound lands at by thinking of a "mirror".

The SP-1200 measures about 26,000 times a second, so the limit it can hold (the ) is 13 kHz. Imagine a mirror standing at 13 kHz. If a 15 kHz sound, 2 kHz above the mirror, gets in without being filtered, it reflects to 11 kHz, 2 kHz below the mirror on the other side. An 11 kHz sound that was never in the original song appears.

That causes something strange. If the original sound goes up from 15 kHz to 16 kHz, the reflection goes down from 11 kHz to 10 kHz. Listen to a sound with lots of highs, like a hi-hat or cymbal, while raising the pitch: everything else goes up, but one metallic tone goes down. That's the reflection.

The way old machines raise the pitch makes this worse. Raising the pitch moves the highs up too, so more sound goes past the mirror. Modern samplers shave off sound that would go past the mirror first, but the SP-1200 doesn't shave anything and just skips samples, so what goes past is reflected straight back in. That's the machine's particular rough flavour.

(As a formula: reflected = sample rate − original frequency. 26 − 15 = 11 kHz.)

Go deeperWhat is nonlinear 12-bit?

A normal ruler has steps that are all the same size. A nonlinear ruler has fine steps for quiet sounds and wide steps for loud ones. The ear is more sensitive to differences in quiet sounds, so with the same 12 bits you can hold quiet sounds more cleanly. It's the same idea as , which is used for phone calls. In return, loud sounds get wide steps and turn a little rough, which adds to the solid feel of that machine's drums.

Go deeperHow did the SNES compress sound?

This sound chip uses a method called . It bundles 16 samples into one block of 9 bytes. The first byte is a header that says how much to scale up this block (the ) and which to use. The other 8 bytes hold the 16 samples at 4 bits each.

4 bits is only 16 steps, so used as is it would be very rough. So it guesses the next value from the one or two samples before, and stores only the gap between the guess and the real value in 4 bits. The gap is smaller than the original value, so even coarse steps do a decent job. On playback it blends 4 neighbouring samples in a bell shape (), which gives the typical softly smeared highs.

In three lines
  • Old samplers sound the way they do because they saved on memory and parts.
  • Low sample rates, coarse bits, aliasing and board filters are those traces.
  • flipper's black, grey and purple engines are modelled on those machines.
8

Playing

Key questionWhat happens inside when you hit a pad?

is sheet music. Pads and keyboards don't send sound. They only send short messages like "note number so-and-so was pressed this hard" and "that note was let go". There are 128 notes, from 0 to 127, and the velocity goes from 1 to 127. When a sampler gets one of these messages, it finds the slice placed on that note and plays it.

Voices Each sound that's ringing right now is called a . Hit a pad three times quickly and three voices can ring over each other.

  • : several voices ring over each other. You need this to play chords.
  • : a new sound cuts off the one before. It feels like jumping around one record, so chop playing stays tidy.
  • : sounds cut each other off only inside a chosen group. It copies what happens on a real drum kit, where hitting the closed hi-hat stops the open hi-hat.

How long does it ring? It can ring only while you hold the pad, or ring to the end of the slice after one hit. A loop goes back to the start when it reaches the end and keeps going round; a rings once and stops.

Envelopes and ADSR The shape of a sound's level as it grows and fades is called its . It's usually split into four stages, named ADSR after their first letters.

  • Attack: the time from pressing the key until the sound reaches its loudest. Short, and it hits right away; long, and it swells in gently.
  • Decay: the time to come down from the loudest point to the sustain level.
  • Sustain: the level the sound stays at while you hold the key. The other three are times; this one alone is a level.
  • Release: the time from letting go of the key until the sound is completely gone. Long, and a tail lingers.

An organ has almost no attack or release, so it sounds the moment you press and stops the moment you let go. A string pad has a long attack and release, so it fades in and fades out. In a sampler, the recording already has its own shape, so you usually only adjust the attack and release. A longer attack softens the head of a drum, and a longer release lets even a short slice end smoothly. In flipper, in and fade out do the job of attack and release.

Playing on a keyboard Spread one slice across the whole keyboard, and thanks to the from chapter 5 each key plays a different pitch. This is how you sample a single piano note and play a melody with it. Choose a and only the notes in that key are laid out, so you can't hit a wrong note even if you don't know any theory.

flipper: try it

  • Pad 1 is C3. The default is mono, so switch to poly, play the same rhythm and hear the difference.
  • Switch between 'while held' and 'whole slice'.
  • In keys mode, set the scale to minor pentatonic and any key you hit will fit.
  • On the drum screen, put two cells in the same choke group.
Go deeperHow do MIDI note numbers connect to frequency?

MIDI gives every note a number. Number 69 is A (440 Hz), and each number up is one up. So 81 is the A an up (880 Hz), and 57 is the A an octave down (220 Hz). Number 60 is middle C.

There's one confusing thing. Depending on the company, number 60 is called C3 or C4. It's the same key with a name one octave apart. If something looks an octave off when you line it up with other gear, this is usually why.

In three lines
  • Pads don't send sound, they send MIDI messages.
  • Mono cuts the last sound, poly lets them overlap, choke cuts within a group.
  • ADSR sets the shape of how a sound starts and ends.
9

Effects and turntables

Key questionWhat part of the sound does an effect change?

Every effect touches one of four things in a sound. Sorting them this way puts all those effects in order at a glance.

What it changesEffectsIn one line
Tone colour (which frequencies are loud)Filter, EQTurns some bands down or up.
How the level moves, Pushes loud parts down so loud and quiet sit closer together.
The shape of the waveDistortion, tape, crushBends or steps the wave, adding overtones that weren't there.
Time and spaceEcho, reverb, chorusCopies the sound and plays it again a little later.

Effects are usually chained one after another. This is called an effect chain. Below is one example; the sound passes through from left to right.

Order matters too Echo after distortion repeats the distorted sound cleanly; distortion after echo distorts the echoes as well. The two sound quite different.

Now let's go one by one.

Filterfilter

A filter cuts away a frequency band. The point where the cutting starts is called the cutoff, and turning the filter knob moves it.

Pick the filter type with the buttons and move the cutoff slider.

  • LP (): lets only the sound below the cutoff through. The highs are cut, so it gets dark and muffled, like music playing in the next room.
  • HP (): lets only the high sound through. The lows drop out, so it gets light and thin.
  • BP (band-pass): keeps only the middle band. It sounds like a phone or a small radio.
  • Slope (12 · 24 dB): how steeply it cuts past the cutoff. The bigger the number, the more firmly it cuts.
  • : lifts the area around the cutoff a little. Turn it up and you get a whistling ring.

Compressorcompressor

A compressor automatically pushes down only the loud sounds that go over a line. Turn the whole thing back up by as much as it was pushed down, and the small hits and tails become louder by comparison, so drums sound solid and close.

Turn the compressor on and the small hits and tails get louder, so the drums firm up. The loudness is matched.

A compressor usually has four knobs.

  • Threshold: only sound above this level gets pushed. It's the dotted line in the picture below.
  • Ratio: how hard to push. At 4:1, whatever goes over is cut to a quarter. A sound 8 dB over the threshold ends up only 2 dB over.
  • Attack: how quickly it starts pushing once the sound goes over. Set it long and the sharp hit at the very start slips through before being pushed, so the hits get sharper.
  • Release: how quickly it lets go once the sound comes back down. Too fast and the sound wobbles; too slow and it's still pushed when the next hit comes.

Turning the whole thing back up by as much as it was pushed down is called makeup . Blend the pushed sound with the original and you keep the life of the original while adding firmness; this is called parallel compression.

Distortiondistortion

Distortion presses down the top of the wave and changes its shape. A new shape brings overtones that weren't there before, so the sound gets thicker and rougher. How it presses changes the flavour.

Five kinds of distortion pushed hard on a clean guitar part played on a Les Paul. The loudness is matched, so compare how rough each one gets.

  • Soft · tube: rounds the top off. Even pushed hard it's less harsh and sounds warm. Tube is modelled on a valve amp.
  • Clip: cuts everything above a set level flat. Rough and sharp.
  • Fold: instead of cutting off what goes over, it folds it back inside. The harder you push, the more metallic it gets.
  • Fuzz: pushes so hard the wave becomes almost square. It sounds like a guitar fuzz pedal.
  • Drive is how much the incoming sound is turned up. The higher, the more it gets pressed and the rougher it sounds. Mix is how much to blend with the original.

Bitcrusherbitcrusher

A bitcrusher makes the traces of old samplers from chapters 2 and 7 on purpose. It lowers how often the sound is measured () and how many steps the ruler has (bits).

Lower the rate and you get metallic tones; lower the bits and you get grit.

  • Rate: repeats each measured value several times, so fewer measurements are made each second. The highs fold back and sound metallic ().
  • Bits: fewer steps on the ruler. The fewer bits, the grittier the quiet sounds.

Tapesaturation

Record loudly onto tape and the tape's magnetism fills up, so the louder the sound, the less it grows. The top of the wave gets gently pressed and the sound turns warm and thick. It's like soft distortion, but much more subtle. An effect that imitates this with calculations is called tape saturation.

The difference is small. Listen to the head of the drums and the lows on headphones.

  • Drive: how loudly it pretends to record onto tape. The higher, the fuller it gets.
  • Wow · flutter: real tape's playback speed wobbles a little, so the pitch sways. It can put a sample's key out, so on samples it's often used very lightly or switched off.

Choruschorus

Chorus mixes in a copy of the sound delayed by a very short time (a few to a few tens of milliseconds). Slowly stretching and shrinking that delay makes the copy's pitch rise and fall slightly, and together with the original it sounds wide and swirling, like several people playing together.

On headphones the sound spreads left and right and swirls a little.

  • Speed (rate): how fast it goes back and forth once. Slow is subtle; fast is wobbly.
  • Depth: how far the delay time swings. The bigger, the more the pitch wobbles.
  • Mix: how much of the copy to blend with the original.

Noisenoise

Noise doesn't change the sound; it lays noise underneath to add an old feel.

Noise only sits underneath. The original sound stays the same.

  • Hiss: the fine noise you hear when tape plays.
  • Crackle: the occasional "pop" on a record.
  • Dust: the tiny sounds of dust sitting on a record.
  • Loud noise blurs the original sound, so it's usually laid in just barely audible.

Echodelay

Echo (delay) copies the sound and plays it again a little later. Feed the repeat back into the echo () and it repeats several times, getting quieter each time. Set the gap to the song's tempo (say, 1/8 beat) and the repeats land right in time.

The echo time is set to the drum loop's tempo (101 BPM). Listen to ping-pong on headphones.

  • Tape echo: like an old tape echo unit, each repeat gets a little darker and blurrier.
  • Digital echo: the repeats stay clean.
  • Ping-pong: the repeats bounce between left and right.
  • Feedback: how much of the repeat goes back in. The higher, the longer it keeps going.

Reverbreverb

Clap in a room and the sound bounces off the walls, floor and ceiling and comes back thousands of times over. Reverb makes this with calculations.

On soul strings and brass. The tail gets longer from room to hall to a huge space. Use the slider to change the balance of the original sound (dry) and the reverb (wet).

  • Room · hall · plate · spring: common kinds of reverb. Room is a small room and hall a big concert hall. Plate and spring were made by ringing a big steel sheet or the spring inside a guitar amp.
  • Decay: the time the reverb tail takes to .
  • Pre-delay: the gap between the original sound and the reverb. A small gap keeps vocals and drums from getting buried in the reverb.
  • Dry · wet: the balance of the original sound (dry) and the reverb (wet).

Finishing: clipper and limitermaster

After all the effects, the level gets a final touch. This is the step that makes the sound loud while keeping it under 0 (the loudest level digital audio can hold, chapter 11).

The more input, the more the tops get cut, so the sound gets denser and rougher. The loudness is matched, so compare the texture, not the level.

  • Clipper: cuts off only the tops that stick out. The more you turn the input up, the more gets cut and the louder and denser the whole thing gets.
  • Limiter: pushes the sound down so it never goes past a set level. It usually sits at the very end to stop sudden loud sound getting out (chapter 11).
  • Width: widens or narrows the stereo with the mid/side from chapter 10.

Effects you holdperformance fx

These change the sound only while you hold them, and it goes back as soon as you let go. Many samplers and DJ units do this with pads or buttons, for quick changes while you play.

On a synth loop. The repeats press and let go of the pad every other beat; the others play one bar as it is and hold the pad for the next bar.

  • Cut: cuts the sound. Cutting and opening in time makes a rhythm.
  • Repeat (stutter): keeps repeating the sound from the moment you pressed, at a set length. The shorter, the more it turns into a "brrr".
  • Stop (brake): pitch and speed drop together, like tape or a record stopping.
  • Back · half · rev: spins the record backwards quickly, plays at half speed (one lower), or plays in reverse.
  • Filter sweep: a filter slowly closes while you hold.
  • Echo throw: sends only the sound while you hold into the echo, and the tail keeps ringing after you let go.

Turntables and scratchingscratch

When you move a record back and forth by hand, how fast the record turns at that moment is the playback speed. Push fast and it's high and fast; push slowly and it's low and slow; pull and it plays backwards. It's the same idea as in chapter 5. Add cutting the sound in and out with the and you get all kinds of scratch techniques. Here are the well-known ones.

  • Baby: push and pull with the fader open. You hear both ways; the most basic scratch.
  • Forward: the fader opens on the push only. You hear only the forward sound.
  • Chirp: shut just before the push ends, open again near the end of the pull. A short, clipped "chirp".
  • Tear: the push in two with a short stop between, then one pull.
  • Transformer: a slow push and pull while the fader opens on every 16th. A robot sound.
  • Flare: the fader open, shut once in the middle of each push. Two sounds a push.
  • 2-click flare: shut twice in each push. Three sounds a push.
  • Crab: four very fast opens on the push, silent on the pull.

flipper: try it

  • The rack in fx mode has ten slots in this order: filter, punch, distortion, crush, tape, chorus, noise, echo, space, master. Set the filter to LP and slowly turn the knob up.
  • Punch is a compressor boiled down to one knob. Hear how far forward the drums come.
  • Put the five kinds of distortion on the same sample one after another.
  • After the master there's a limiter that's always on, so no setting can go past −0.3 dBFS.
  • Spin the platter with the mouse, and press the fx pads and the eight scratch patterns.
In three lines
  • An effect changes tone colour, how the level moves, the wave's shape, or time and space.
  • The same effects sound different in a different order.
  • When scratching, how fast you push the record is the playback speed.
10

Stereo

Key questionWhat are left, right, mid and side?

A stereo sample holds two lines of sound: one for the left speaker and one for the right. Sound that's the same in both lines is heard in the middle, and sound in only one line is heard on that side.

You can also split these two lines another way.

  • Mid = (left + right) ÷ 2. The sound the two lines share, that is, the sound in the middle. Vocals, kick and bass usually sit here.
  • Side = (left − right) ÷ 2. The part where the two lines differ. The middle sound cancels out the moment you subtract, leaving wide reverb, double-tracked parts and instruments panned to one side.

The ÷ 2 is there so the sound doesn't get louder than it was.

A loop mixed wide like a 1970s soul record. Listen on headphones. With side alone, the middle drops out and only the spread-out sound is left.

What's it for? Listen to the side alone and the vocal in the middle drops right down; pick one channel and you can use an instrument recorded only on that side by itself. This is especially handy with 1960s–70s records, which often have the drums on one side and the vocal on the other.

It has limits too Mid/side isn't a way to pull instruments apart. Everything in the middle goes to mid and everything spread out goes to side, so if the vocal and guitar are both in the middle, they come along together. A sound that only uses the side disappears when summed to .

flipper: try it

  • On a stereo sample, press the 'oo' key and the splits into two lines, left and right. Look for sounds that are only on one side.
  • In the channel menu, listen to stereo, left, right, mid and side in turn. Anything other than stereo goes out in mono.
Go deeperFrom mid and side back to left and right

Add mid and side and you get left; subtract and you get right. Left = mid + side, right = mid − side. So splitting into mid/side and putting it back together gives exactly the original sound. Turn up just the side and the sound gets wider; turn it down and it gathers in the middle.

Summed to mono, left + right = mid × 2, and the side cancels out. That means anything only in the side can't be heard where sound comes out in mono, like in a club or on a phone speaker. If you widened something with the side, listen to it in mono too.

A boom bap loop with the bass and kick in the middle. Summed to mono, the bass and kick stay; with side alone they almost vanish.

In three lines
  • Stereo is two channels, left and right.
  • Mid is what they share; side is how they differ.
  • Summed to mono, the side disappears. That's why bass stays in the middle.
11

Loudness and safety

Key questionWhy is a sudden loud sound dangerous?

Digital has a ceiling. The top step of the ruler from chapter 2 is the ceiling, called 0 . Every level is written as how far below the ceiling it is, as a negative number (like −6 dBFS). Sound that goes past the ceiling gets its top cut off and turns harsh. This is called .

  • : turning the sound up or down. +6 makes the wave about twice as tall.
  • : the loudest moment in a sound. To avoid clipping, watch the peak.
  • : setting the gain so the peak touches the ceiling. Use it to bring a quietly recorded sample up to a similar level as the others.
  • How loud it feels: even with the same peak, a sound that rings longer feels louder. So when comparing two sounds, match how loud they feel first. Whichever is even a little louder will seem better for no real reason.

Why is a sudden loud sound dangerous? If a plugin suddenly makes a loud sound while your headphones or monitors are turned up, it can damage your ears or speakers. It's often caused by (sound going back in and building up) or a calculation error.

Three habits

  1. Start a session with the volume down and turn it up bit by bit.
  2. Turn knobs that can make sound build up, like echo repeats or , slowly.
  3. A on the master is your last safety net.

flipper: try it

  • Watch the meter on the top row. A dot lights up when the sound hits the top.
  • Press normalize on a quietly recorded sample. The sample gain goes up by that much.
  • Set the limiter in the fx rack's master to 'safe' and it only catches sound above −0.3 dBFS.
Go deeperHow do you work out dB?

dB is a unit that turns "how many times bigger" into adding. There are only two to remember: twice as big is +6 dB, and ten times as big is +20 dB. The other way, half is −6 dB. Because it's adding, it's handy: +6 dB twice is +12 dB, which is 2 × 2 = 4 times. (As a formula it's 20 × log10(ratio), and putting in 2 gives about 6.02, so "6 dB".)

Each step is 6 dB, so the level halves every time.

0 dBFS is the ceiling, so −6 dBFS is about half the ceiling, and −20 dBFS is a tenth.

Go deeperWhy set a limiter at −0.3 dBFS instead of 0?

Digital numbers are dots, and the sound that comes out of the speaker is a smooth curve joining them. All the dots can be under the ceiling while the curve between two dots goes slightly over. This is called an inter-sample peak (). Peaks also rise a little when converting to formats like MP3.

So the last safety net goes a little below the ceiling, usually between −0.3 and −1 dBFS.

How loud a song feels is measured separately, in a unit called . It measures the average loudness the ear hears rather than the peak, and streaming services use it to match the level of every song.

In three lines
  • Digital has a ceiling called 0 dBFS.
  • Half the size is 6 dB quieter.
  • Start with the volume low and let a limiter guard the end.
12

Samples and copyright

Key questionWhich samples can you use?

This chapter isn't legal advice. It differs from country to country and contract to contract, so if anything worries you before releasing a song, ask a professional. Here we only cover the basics.

A song carries two kinds of rights. One is the right to the composition, held by the songwriters who wrote the melody and lyrics. The other is the right to the recording, held by whoever performed and recorded the song and made the master. That's usually the label or company that paid for the recording. If the singer didn't write the song, they may hold neither right.

Taylor Swift's case shows clearly that the two are separate. Swift wrote her songs herself, so she held the rights to the compositions, but the rights to the recordings of her old albums stayed with the label she first signed to. So she recorded the same songs again from scratch and released them as "Taylor's Version". The song is the same, but the new sound is a new recording, and Swift holds the rights to it.

Taking a sample from a record usually touches both rights. So to share your song with others, even for free, in principle you have to go one of two ways.

  • Sample clearance: contact both the songwriters' side and the label that owns the recording, and get permission to use the sample. Usually you pay or share income.
  • Re-recording (replay): hire musicians to play that part again closely and record it fresh. Like Swift, the recording is new, so you don't need the label's permission. But the melody is the same, so you still need the songwriters' permission.

If several people wrote the song, you need permission from all of them. Permission from the singer alone isn't enough.

Outside Korea there are many cases of uncleared samples going to court.

  • Biz Markie (1991, USA): lost a case over sampling a Gilbert O'Sullivan song without permission. The album was pulled from shops, and after this ruling sample clearance became standard practice in American hip-hop.
  • Bridgeport v. Dimension Films (2005, USA): the court ruled that even a 2-second guitar sound with its pitch changed needs permission. The ruling left behind the line "Get a license or do not sample."
  • The Verve, "Bitter Sweet Symphony" (1997, UK): they used more of an orchestral version of a Rolling Stones song than they had permission for, and had to hand over the song's income and songwriting credit for over 20 years. They only got it back in 2019.
  • Kanye West: uses a lot of samples and clears most of them, but has been sued several times over ones he didn't. "The Joy" (2011) brought a suit from soul singer Syl Johnson, and "New Slaves" (2013) one from Gábor Presser, who wrote the song by the Hungarian band Omega; both were settled. For "Good (Don't Die)" (2024) he asked Donna Summer's estate to use "I Feel Love", was refused, had the melody sung again and released it anyway. He was sued and settled. It shows that re-recording still needs separate permission for the composition (the melody).

So rights holders can sue anyone who used their work without permission at any time. Most cases don't reach a ruling, though, and end in a paid settlement.

In Korea it's hard to find public cases of sampling going all the way to a ruling. Disputes mostly turn into plagiarism rows, and sample permission is often settled by people in the industry contacting each other directly. So from the outside the process is hard to see. That doesn't mean the rules are different. Korean copyright law also protects the composition and the recording separately, so the principle is the same as elsewhere.

Is uncleared sampling OK on SoundCloud or a mixtape?Q&A

In principle, no. Whether you get paid or post it for free, sharing someone else's song and recording with people is the same thing, and it needs permission.

Lots of mixtapes and remixes still go up, not because it's OK, but because rights holders don't make an issue of it or let it slide as promotion. So things like this can happen.

  • Your track suddenly comes down from SoundCloud. If it happens several times, your account gets blocked.
  • On YouTube, the track's ad income goes to the original's owners, or the video gets blocked.
  • If the track gets famous later, you can be sued then. That goes for tracks you posted for free too.

The realistic path

  • For practice or tracks only you listen to, sample anything you like. If you don't share it, it isn't a problem.
  • For tracks you share, use sounds you recorded yourself or sample packs.
  • If there's an old song you really want to use, talk to a professional before you share it.

Sample packs and instrument sounds Royalty-free sample packs, sounds that come with your , and presets usually come with conditions like these.

  • Putting them in your own song and releasing it is fine.
  • Pulling the sounds out on their own and handing them out (selling them as a sample pack, sharing them as files) isn't.
  • Handing them out after tweaking them a little is usually blocked too.

The exact conditions differ by product, so always read that product's license.

The safest sound is one you made yourself. Sounds you recorded yourself, and sounds you built from scratch on a synthesizer without a , are yours, so you can use them in songs and hand them out as one-shots.

flipper: try it

  • With the record key on the empty screen, record your , objects you tap, or an instrument you play, and chop it. It's entirely your own sample.
In three lines
  • A song has a right to the composition and a separate right to the recording.
  • Sharing a song needs permission, even for free.
  • The safest sample is a sound you made yourself.
+

Wrapping up

That was a lot to read. Thanks for staying with it all the way to the end! You now have a foundation in samplers, digital recording and computer music. With solid basics, whatever new gear or feature you run into, you'll know the principle behind it and it will make sense quickly. Go make some great music. 🎉🎉

  • Lyn Collins – "Think (About It)" (1972): famous for its "Woo! Yeah!" shout and its break.open ↗
  • The Honey Drippers – "Impeach the President" (1973): a break famous for its short, hard kick and snare.open ↗
  • Incredible Bongo Band – "Apache" (1973): a bongo and drum break. Early hip-hop DJs looped it with two copies of the record.open ↗
  • Bob James – "Nautilus" (1974): its dark keyboard intro has been used in countless hip-hop songs.open ↗

Every word in the pop-ups The notes that open when you press a coloured, dotted-underlined word in the text, in alphabetical order.

ADC analog-to-digital converter
The part that measures the electrical vibration at a steady pace and turns it into numbers.
aliasing
Sound above the limit a sample rate can hold folding back down to a lower place, making tones that were never there.
autocorrelation
Sliding a signal over itself bit by bit and measuring how alike the two are. Used to find repeating gaps like beats or pitch.
bit depth
How many steps each measurement can land on. 16 bits gives 65,536 steps.
BPM beats per minute
How many beats come in one minute. The unit of tempo.
BRR Bit Rate Reduction
The SNES sound chip's compression. It packs 16 samples (32 bytes) into 9 bytes, about 3.6 times smaller.
cent
A very small pitch unit: one semitone split into 100 steps.
choke
Within a chosen group, a new sound cuts off the one before it.
chroma
A bar chart of how much each of the twelve notes sounded, ignoring octaves.
clipping
The harsh sound made when the top of a wave past the ceiling (0 dBFS) gets cut off.
compressor
An effect that turns loud parts down so loud and quiet sit closer together.
correlation
How closely two lists rise and fall together, from −1 to 1. At 1 they have exactly the same shape.
crossfader
The sideways slider on a DJ mixer. It cuts the sound in and out quickly.
DAC digital-to-analog converter
The part that turns numbers back into a smooth electrical vibration. It sits before your headphones and speakers.
DAW Digital Audio Workstation
The program you make songs in, like Logic, Ableton or FL Studio.
dB decibel
A unit for the difference in level between two sounds. +6 dB makes the wave about twice as big.
dBFS decibels full scale
Digital level measured down from the ceiling (0 dBFS), so it's always negative. −6 dBFS is about half the ceiling.
drum break
A part of a song where the other instruments drop out and only the drums play. A favourite source for hip-hop sampling.
envelope
The shape of a sound's level as it starts, holds and fades away.
equal temperament
Tuning that splits an octave into twelve semitones of exactly the same ratio. Most instruments today use it.
fade
Raising the sound gradually (fade in) or lowering it gradually (fade out).
feedback
Sound going back into its own input and building up.
frame
One short piece of sound cut out for analysis, usually tens of milliseconds long.
frequency
How many times per second something vibrates, written in Hz. The higher the number, the higher the note.
frequency resolution
How well you can tell two close frequencies apart. Longer frames give better frequency resolution.
gain
How much the sound is turned up or down.
Gaussian
A bell-shaped curve: high in the middle, gently lower on both sides. Used as weights so nearer samples count more.
high-pass
A filter that cuts sound below a set frequency. The sound gets lighter.
interpolation
A calculation that guesses the values between two samples and fills them in.
key profile
A table of how often each of the 24 keys uses each note.
kHz kilohertz
A thousand vibrations (or measurements) per second.
Lazy Chop
Cutting by tapping keys while the sound plays. It lines each cut up with the nearest transient.
limiter
A strong compressor that never lets the sound go past a set level.
low-pass
A filter that cuts sound above a set frequency. The sound gets darker.
LUFS Loudness Units relative to Full Scale
A unit for the average loudness the ear hears. Streaming services use it to match songs (for example −14 LUFS).
MIDI Musical Instrument Digital Interface
An agreement for instruments to say "this note was pressed this hard". It carries messages, not sound.
mono
Sound kept in one channel. Left and right speakers play exactly the same thing.
nonlinear
Measuring quiet and loud sounds on steps of different sizes.
normalize
Turning the whole sound up until its peak touches the ceiling.
Nyquist frequency
Half the sample rate. Anything higher can't be stored correctly.
octave
The distance where the frequency exactly doubles (or halves). From one C to the next C.
one-shot
A sound that plays once to its end when you hit it.
overtone
The higher tones that ring along inside one note. They decide the tone colour.
peak
The level of the loudest moment in a sound.
phantom power
48 V sent down the mic cable to power a condenser mic. Switched on with the 48V button on the interface.
phase
Where a repeating wave is right now: on the way up, at the top, and so on.
phase vocoder
A time stretch method that splits sound into frequencies with the FFT and keeps each one's phase lined up while stretching.
poly
A mode where several sounds can ring over each other.
preamp
A device that turns a microphone's very weak signal up to a level you can record.
prediction filter
A calculation that guesses the next sample from the last few. Storing only the gap between guess and truth takes fewer bits.
preset
A saved instrument or effect setting made ahead of time.
repitch
Changing the reading speed so pitch and speed change together, like spinning a record faster.
resonance
How much a filter boosts the edge frequency. Turn it up and you hear a whistling ring.
royalty-free
You pay once and never pay again each time you use it in a song.
sample rate
How many times per second the sound is measured. 44.1 kHz means 44,100 times a second.
scale
The set of notes used in a key. For example, minor pentatonic.
semitone
The step from one piano key to the very next one. Twelve semitones make an octave.
sensitivity
How clear a jump has to be before it counts as a transient. Higher catches quieter sounds.
shift
Making a number 2, 4, 8… times bigger or smaller (moving its bits sideways). In BRR it says how much to scale each block's 4-bit values.
spectrum
How much of each frequency a sound contains, laid out side by side. The moving bars on an EQ screen.
synthesizer
An instrument that builds sound from scratch with circuits or calculations.
time resolution
How finely you can tell when a sound happened. Shorter frames give better time resolution.
time stretch
Changing only the length (speed) of a sound while the pitch stays put.
transient
The sharp hit at the very start of a sound. Also called the attack.
true peak
The real top of the wave once the gaps between samples are redrawn smoothly. Can sit a little above the highest sample.
voice
One sound that is ringing right now.
waveform
A line drawing of how the sound's level changes over time. The wavy shape on screen.
zero crossing
A spot where the waveform passes through the middle line (0). Cutting there makes no click.
μ-law
A nonlinear scale that gives quiet sounds more steps. It was made to fit voices into 8 bits on phone lines.

Sounds on this page The loops in the listening examples (drums, piano, soul, synth, guitar) were made with Suno. The scratch sounds were rendered ahead of time with flipper's scratch engine. The other sounds (the sine waves, the bass and the single synth note) are calculated by this page itself.
